Evidence-backed Authorization Decision Analysis
for SAGA
Abstract
Policy-governed agent communication requires authorization deci-
sions to preserve intended policy semantics across evaluation and en-
forcement. Authentication and confidentiality alone do not establish
this consistency. We investigate the requirement through a SAGA case
study. Archived direct calls to the unmodified contact-policy matcher
demonstrate an order-dependent authorization decision inconsistency:
a specific-deny/general-allow rulebook yields an allow-side budget al-
though documented most-specific semantics select denial. Separately,
a diagnostic extension retains the queried authentication correspon-
dences and token secrecy while an added authorization correspondence
is false. This identifies a verification-coverage gap, not a formal proof
of the matcher inconsistency. For the recorded policy input, an inde-
pendent finite specification evaluator derives Deny, while the archived
matcher observation supplies Allow. A decision bridge checks the corre-
sponding recorded policy input and observation provenance, constructs
the decision pair, and reconstructs the fixed authorization-divergence
scenario analyzed in the archived ProVerif 2.05 run. Under its explicit
symbolic assumptions, the derived model admits application-message
acceptance (ChatAccept) and establishes that acceptance implies prior
token issuance (TokenIssue). Independent gate controls distinguish
Provider and receiver blocking stages. These results connect imple-
mentation observations to symbolic consequences through checked ev-
idence transfer for the recorded case. They establish neither crypto-
graphic compromise nor deployed-service reproduction. Mapping the
concrete evaluation to symbolic participants remains an explicit ab-
straction; general implementation-to-model refinement and correctness
for arbitrary policies remain unproved.

1. Introduction
LLM-based agents increasingly use external tools and ser-
vices [1], [2]. Authentication establishes identity, whereas
receiver-side authorization determines whether the identified
agent may communicate [3]. Authentication and token se-
crecy alone do not establish compliance with the receiver’s
intended contact policy.
SAGA [4] governs communication between registered
agents using contact policies and access-control tokens. Its
policy matcher implements the receiver’s authorization de-
cision. We investigate:Can a mismatch between the re-
ceiver’s intended policy and its implementation permit a
denied agent, and how far can that permission propagate
through the protocol?
We identify an order-dependent matcher defect that vi-
olates SAGA’s most-specific-rule semantics, yielding spec-
ification denial but implementation permission. An au-
thorization coverage diagnostic identifies a missing proof
obligation without discovering the implementation defect.
Controlled executions of production Provider and receiver
code paths confirm propagation to token issuance and stor-
age. Under the corresponding evidence-linked fixed sym-
bolic divergence, ProVerif reportsChatAcceptreachable
while the prior-TokenIssuecorrespondence holds. Actual
application-message acceptance is not established.
Our contributions are (1) identifying and explaining
a concrete authorization decision inconsistency in SAGA;
(2) analyzing its conditional symbolic consequences using
ProVerif; and (3) validating its propagation to token issuance
and storage through controlled production-code execution.

secret key holder and the user issuing the query may be dif-

etal.[2]proposedpublickeyencryptionwithobliviouskey-

from the key holder without revealing their keywords. They
applied PEOKS to build a public key encrypted database
supporting authorized private searches.
Han,Han,Meng,Lai,andWu[3]consideredtraceabil-
ity (by another entity called a tracer) in the PEOKS context
and proposed a pairing-based scheme. Hereafter, we call
it the HHMLW scheme. Han et al. introduced a trapdoor
generation center (TGC) that has a secret key for generating
trapdoors. They claimed that the HHMLW scheme ensures
keyword blindness, guaranteeing that the TGC generates a
trapdoor without knowledge of the keyword.
Our Contribution. In this short note, we show that their
scheme does not provide keyword blindness. Our attack is
eﬃcient, as it involves only elliptic curve computations and
does not require any pairing operations. We emphasize that
our attack follows their security model.

Abstract—Forced by regulations and industry demand, banks
worldwide are working to open their customers’ online banking
accounts to third-party services via web-based APIs. By using
these so-called Open Banking APIs, third-party companies, such
as FinTechs, are able to read information about and initiate
payments from their users’ bank accounts. Such access to
ﬁnancial data and resources needs to meet particularly high
security requirements to protect customers.
One of the most promising standards in this segment is the
OpenID Financial-grade API (F API) , currently under develop-
ment in an open process by the OpenID Foundation and backed
by large industry partners. The FAPI is a proﬁle of OAuth 2.0
designed for high-risk scenarios and aiming to be secure against
very strong attackers. To achieve this level of security, the FAPI
employs a range of mechanisms that have been developed to
harden OAuth 2.0, such as Code and T oken Binding (including
mTLS and OAUTB), JWS Client Assertions , and Proof Key for
Code Exchange .
In this paper, we perform a rigorous, systematic formal analy-
sis of the security of the FAPI, based on an existing comprehensive
model of the web infrastructure—the Web Infrastructure Model
(WIM) proposed by Fett, Küsters, and Schmitz. To this end, we
ﬁrst develop a precise model of the FAPI in the WIM, including
different proﬁles for read-only and read-write access, different
ﬂows, different types of clients, and different combinations of
security features, capturing the complex interactions in a web-
based environment. We then use our model of the FAPI to
precisely deﬁne central security properties. In an attempt to
prove these properties, we uncover partly severe attacks, breaking
authentication, authorization, and session integrity properties.
We develop mitigations against these attacks and ﬁnally are able
to formally prove the security of a ﬁxed version of the FAPI.
Although ﬁnancial applications are high-stakes environments,
this work is the ﬁrst to formally analyze and, importantly, verify
an Open Banking security proﬁle.
By itself, this analysis is an important contribution to the
development of the FAPI since it helps to deﬁne exact security
properties
